title: This Office Was the Best Defense Against Discrimination in Schools. Trump Destroyed It. discrimination-in-schools/
author: Chris Lewis
summary: Chris Lewis of the Revolving Door Project argues that the Trump administration has hollowed out the Education Department's Office for Civil Rights, not only by freezing investigations but by dismantling the low-cost tools that once resolved problems before they escalated. He opens with a frozen complaint about racial slurs directed at a Black fifth grader in Michigan, and notes that OCR has reached only three settlements since the administration took over. Lewis focuses on OCR's technical assistance program, which answered 11,000 inquiries and gave 211 presentations in 2024, and on the Equity Assistance Centers, successors to 1960s desegregation centers, whose grants were terminated and whose regulations the department proposed to rescind. He cites the department's own data showing those centers exceeded their targets, and warns that shifting enforcement to the Justice Department cannot replicate the OCR model, leaving teachers and families with fewer avenues for resolving civil rights disputes.
points: OCR has reached only three settlements since the Trump administration took office, while dozens of near-complete cases were frozen.
Seven of OCR's 12 regional offices, which provided on-site civil rights training, were shuttered.
In 2024 OCR responded to 11,000 inquiries and conducted 211 technical assistance presentations.
More than 120 districts remain under active federal desegregation orders, yet all four Equity Assistance Center grants were terminated.
Four in five districts reported increased awareness after Equity Assistance Center help, exceeding the department's own targets.
quotes: While the OCR is still pursuing cases, the office has been flipped on its head —turned into a political weapon aimed at perceived threats to modern conservatism, reflected in its focus on investigating trans athletes or alleged racism against white students.
The OCR has easy-to-implement tools to resolve many civil rights issues without a full investigation, namely the Office for Civil Rights’ technical assistance program.

Such technical training often helped prevent disputes before they even happened, or resolved them at an early stage without need for courts or hearings. Seven of the 12 offices were shuttered last year.
In 2024, OCR responded to 11,000 inquiries and conducted 211 technical assistance presentations.

Taken together, the grant terminations, proposed elimination of funding, and potential regulatory changes represent a sustained effort to dismantle the federal infrastructure that has provided schools with civil rights technical assistance for decades.
As federal technical assistance capacity diminishes, schools and families are left with fewer avenues for resolving civil rights disputes.
